details:
**Leaves of Grass**
Whitman's life work, a poetry collection first self-published in 1855 with just twelve untitled poems. He revised and expanded it for the rest of his life, ending with the 1891–92 "deathbed edition." It is the most common giveaway for him and contains nearly all of his famous poems.

**"Song of Myself"**
Whitman's most famous poem, the long free-verse centerpiece of Leaves of Grass, divided into 52 sections. It opens "I celebrate myself, and sing myself" and includes "I loafe and invite my soul." In section 6 a child asks "What is the grass?" and the speaker guesses it is "the beautiful uncut hair of graves"; the poem ends "I stop somewhere waiting for you."

**"I sound my barbaric yawp over the roofs of the world"**
A famous line near the end of "Song of Myself," just after the speaker declares "I too am untranslatable." It sums up Whitman's loud, untamed, distinctly American voice.

**"I am large, I contain multitudes" and "every atom belonging to me as good belongs to you"**
Two signature lines from "Song of Myself." The first answers the charge that the speaker contradicts himself ("Very well then I contradict myself"); the second, from the opening, expresses Whitman's democratic identification with every reader. The poem also states "to die is different from what any one supposed, and luckier."

**"O Captain! My Captain!"**
Whitman's elegy for Abraham Lincoln, unusual in his work for its rhyme and meter. It casts Lincoln as a ship's captain who dies just as "our fearful trip is done"; the speaker sees "the bleeding drops of red" where his Captain lies on the deck "fallen cold and dead," while the shore exults and bells ring.

**"When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom'd"**
Whitman's longer elegy for Lincoln, built around three symbols: the lilac, the "great star" that "early droop'd in the western sky" (the "powerful western fallen star," Lincoln), and a hermit thrush singing in a swamp. It was first published in Sequel to Drum-Taps, and its speaker mourns "with ever-returning spring." He also wrote the short Lincoln poem "Hush'd Be the Camps To-day."

**"Crossing Brooklyn Ferry"**
A poem set on the ferry over the East River between Manhattan and Brooklyn. It opens "Flood-tide below me! I see you face to face!" and describes sea-gulls "oscillating their bodies." It speaks directly to future "men and women of a generation" who will cross after him, asking what the count of years between them matters, and ends saying the objects "furnish your parts toward the soul."

**"Out of the Cradle Endlessly Rocking"**
Originally titled "A Child's Reminiscence," this poem describes a boy on the beach of Paumanok (Long Island) who hears a mockingbird mourn its lost mate in italicized songs. The poem ends with the sea whispering the word "death," and its final words are "the sea whisper'd me."

**"I Sing the Body Electric"**
A poem celebrating the human body as inseparable from the soul. It describes a common farmer who is the father of five sons, includes "the armies of those I love engirth me," asks "if the body were not the soul, what is the soul?", and ends "O I say now these are the soul!" Ray Bradbury named a short story collection after it.

**"When I Heard the Learn'd Astronomer"**
A short poem in which the speaker, shown the "proofs, the figures" "ranged in columns" at a lecture, grows "tired and sick." He wanders out into the "mystical moist night-air" and "look'd up in perfect silence at the stars," preferring direct experience to scientific analysis.

**"A Noiseless Patient Spider"**
A short poem comparing a spider that "launch'd forth filament, filament, filament, out of itself" to the speaker's soul, "surrounded, detached, in measureless oceans of space," which seeks connection with the world.

**Drum-Taps and "The Wound Dresser"**
Drum-Taps (1865) is Whitman's collection of Civil War poems, inspired by his work as a volunteer nurse in Washington hospitals. "The Wound Dresser" describes tending the hurt and wounded "with soothing hand," and "Beat! Beat! Drums!" cries "blow! bugles! blow!"

**The "Calamus" poems**
A cluster of poems in Leaves of Grass celebrating "manly love" and comradeship between men. They are the most open expression of Whitman's homosexuality and include "Are You the New Person Drawn Toward Me?", which warns "it may be all maya, illusion."

**Allen Ginsberg's "A Supermarket in California"**
Ginsberg imagines Whitman as a "lonely old grubber, poking among the meats" and "eyeing the grocery boys" in a supermarket. He asks "Where are we going, Walt Whitman?" and "which way does your beard point tonight?"

**Tributes by other poets**
Many poets have written to or about Whitman. Ezra Pound's "A Pact" makes "a truce" with him after detesting him "long enough"; Federico García Lorca's "Ode to Walt Whitman" calls him a "lovely old man" with a "beard full of butterflies"; Rubén Darío wrote a sonnet to him, Pablo Neruda an ode, and Sherman Alexie the poem "Defending Walt Whitman." E. M. Forster took the title A Passage to India from Whitman's poem "Passage to India."
